name: Face slimming supplements / teas
lead: Face slimming supplements and teas are herbal products marketed or discussed as a way to reduce facial puffiness or fat, usually through claims of diuretic, laxative, metabolism-boosting or detox effects. They are sold under the broader heading of herbal and dietary weight-loss products.

In the United States, herbal teas are treated as food products that must be safe to consume but are not required to show evidence of efficacy.[1] No published human trial found in the sources reviewed has tested any tea or supplement specifically for reducing facial fat.[1][2]
Documented safety concerns with weight-loss herbal products include contamination and drug interactions with some herbs, and the 2004 US ban of ephedra-containing supplements.[1][2]
infobox: Food or supplement; efficacy not required

paras: Products in this group include herbal teas, tea blends sold as detox or slimming teas, and capsules containing botanical extracts. Marketing generally says they reduce water retention, suppress appetite or speed fat metabolism, and some appearance forums say this leads to a leaner face.

Encyclopedic sources note that US regulation treats herbal teas as foods that must be safe, without a requirement to demonstrate that they work.[1] They report that herbal teas may contain pesticides or heavy metals depending on source, and that some herbs interact with drugs through liver enzymes; St. John's wort is contraindicated with certain medications such as oral contraceptives.[1] Comfrey is described as potentially harmful to the liver with chronic use, and several herbs are advised against in pregnancy.[1]

Ephedra, a plant extract containing the stimulant ephedrine, was sold as a weight-loss supplement and was banned in the United States in 2004 over concerns about raised blood pressure and risk of stroke and death.[2] Phenylpropanolamine, an over-the-counter ingredient, was withdrawn in 2005 because of risk of hemorrhagic stroke.[2] A review of anti-obesity drugs withdrawn between 1964 and 2009 found that most acted on brain neurotransmitters and were pulled mainly for psychiatric, cardiac or dependence problems.[2]

A meta-analysis cited in encyclopedic sources found an average loss of about 1.9 kg with ephedrine, and ephedrine combined with caffeine was associated with estimated losses of about 4 to 6 kg.[2] These figures concern whole-body weight and a product no longer legally sold as a US supplement; they say nothing about facial fat.[2]
Research on spot reduction, the idea that a treatment can target fat in one area, generally reports that fat loss is not site-specific.[3]
No studies found. No published trial in the sources reviewed has examined slimming teas or herbal supplements for facial fat. Studies of ephedrine for whole-body weight are described above.[2]

timeline.event: Ephedra-containing supplements banned in the United States.[2]
Phenylpropanolamine withdrawn from the US over-the-counter market.[2]

card.summary: Herbal teas and capsules sold for a slimmer face; no trial has tested them for facial fat and some herbal slimming ingredients have been banned.
card.note: Herbal products are not required to show efficacy in the US; some ingredients have drug interactions or were withdrawn.

quick.overview:
Face slimming teas and supplements are herbal products promoted for reducing puffiness or facial fat, often with diuretic or detox claims.

No trial found has tested them for the face. Encyclopedic sources note that US herbal teas need only be safe, not proven effective.
quick.mechanism: Marketing cites water loss, appetite suppression or faster metabolism. Research on spot reduction generally reports that fat loss is not targeted to one body area.
quick.risks: Documented concerns include contamination, drug interactions with some herbs, and past bans such as ephedra in 2004. Individual products vary widely.
